title: What doesn't belong
briefing: The audit continues. app-01 is a web/database box, so its installed packages
should be web, database and system tooling — nothing that helps an attacker.
One installed package in the 'net' section stands out: an old netcat whose
-e option can hand someone a shell. Find it by name.
tips: Look in the net-related packages for the classic netcat (its description mentions spawning shells).
objective: Identify the risky netcat package that's installed and write its exact package name to ~/risky.txt.
expert_objective: Name the installed package that shouldn't be on a server; put it in ~/risky.txt.
hints: List what's installed: `apt list --installed` (or `dpkg -l`). Scan the net section.
It's the traditional netcat — the description warns that -e can spawn shells.
explanation: Auditing installed software is core hardening: attackers love tools that are already present ('living off the land'). netcat-traditional's -e flag turns it into a ready-made backdoor, so on a server it's exactly the kind of thing a review should flag.
